title: Threads vs Processes and the Scheduler
oneLiner: What a process owns, what its threads share, and how the OS slices one CPU core between many threads.
keyTakeaway: A process owns an address space (the memory it can see: its code, heap and globals), open file handles and other OS resources; a thread owns only a stack, its registers (the CPU's working slots) and an instruction pointer (where it is in the code), and shares everything else with the other threads in its process. Sharing memory is what makes threads cheap to create and to switch between, and it is also exactly why they need locks. The scheduler gives each runnable thread a short time slice, then saves its registers and loads another thread's: a context switch.
explanation:
A process is a running program plus everything the OS has handed it: a private virtual address space (its code, its heap, its global and static data), a table of open files and sockets (network connections), environment variables, a user identity and security token. Two processes cannot read each other's memory unless they deliberately set up shared memory or talk through pipes, sockets or files. That isolation is why one crashed browser tab does not take down the others, and why starting a process is comparatively expensive: the OS has to build a whole new address space.

A thread is one path of execution inside a process. Every process starts with one thread, and can start more. Each thread gets its own stack (a scratch area of memory for its local variables and the frames of the calls in progress; see Stack vs Heap and Garbage Collection), its own copy of the CPU registers and its own instruction pointer, but all the threads in a process share the same heap (the area where objects live), the same statics and the same open files. In C#, two threads that can reach the same object are touching the very same bytes in memory, with nothing between them. That is the whole reason race conditions exist.

A CPU core runs one thread at a time. The OS scheduler keeps a queue of runnable (ready) threads and gives each one a time slice, often a few milliseconds. When the slice runs out, or the thread blocks on I/O or a lock, the scheduler performs a context switch: it saves the current thread's registers and instruction pointer, picks the next ready thread, and restores that thread's saved registers. A blocked thread is not in the ready queue at all, so it costs no CPU while it waits. Switching between threads of the same process is cheaper than switching between processes, because the address space stays the same and the CPU's address translation cache (the TLB) stays useful.

Concurrency and parallelism are different words. Concurrency means several tasks are in progress at once, possibly by taking turns on one core. Parallelism means they literally run at the same instant on different cores. Turn the core count down to 1 below and you still get concurrency, just no parallelism. In .NET you rarely create raw Thread objects: Task.Run and the thread pool reuse a small set of threads, because each thread reserves its own stack (1 MB by default on Windows) plus a kernel object.

Interview phrasing to have ready: "processes are isolated and communicate through IPC (inter-process communication: pipes, sockets, shared memory); threads share memory and communicate through it, which is faster but needs synchronization." For the hardware underneath (cores, RAM, the OS boundary) see Computer Architecture in Computer Fundamentals.
